The Caravan Physician's World A physician crossing Veydria in 1300 carries: a humoral or energetic framework for balance, a small travelling case of dried simples and distilled oils, a lancet, a cautery iron, a cupping horn, and bandages. What changes from region to region is not her craft but her eyes: the sign-clusters she recognises, the plants within a day's walk, and the ailments she has been taught to name. Design philosophy: Ecology is real; magic does not touch it. No germ theory, no microscope, no anaesthesia beyond opium/mandrake/hemp/henbane/alcohol, no surgical asepsis beyond wine/vinegar/honey. Childhood mortality is high because it was; chronic illness is common because it was; occupational disease is a moral fact of ordinary work. The Rahab and Arwat rahab (Camelus dromedarius, dromedary pack camel; plural ruhub) and arwat (aristocratic riding breed). Names preserved verbatim — no alteration, no alternative proposed. Co-Evolutionary History The Irrah interior is hyper-arid and forbids any economy that cannot walk from oasis to oasis. The camel's physiology is the solution: oval red blood cells that circulate through dehydrated blood without clumping; selective brain-cooling via the carotid rete; tolerance of 30-40% body-weight water loss; the ability to drink 140 liters in a single session; a fat hump decoupled from water storage; nasal passages that recover exhaled moisture. Two functionally distinct lines from the same species: - rahab — stocky, broad-chested, carrying 150-250 kg at caravan pace for weeks between wells - arwat — light-skeletoned, deep-girthed, "greyhound-bellied," bred for speed and endurance under a single rider The two lines interbreed but the distinction is maintained by ownership lineage. One does not load a known arwat with trade goods; one does not ride a rahab to one's own wedding. Cultural Role The rahab moves desert commerce — salt, dates, textiles, glass, copper — along…

The Tokhan Horse Tokhan [PROP] (Equus ferus caballus, Mongolian-type landrace). Back-harmony vowels u and a, voiced uvular fricative gh, final nasal n typical of Kheshkai animate nouns. Plural: turghat (collective suffix). Phonological note: Revised from original "Turghan" proposal (which contained forbidden /r/). Tokhan uses back-harmony /o/ + /a/ with no liquid consonants. Co-Evolutionary History The Kheshkai steppe swings from -40 C winter to +40 C summer, and the turghan survives the full swing without shelter. Small (12-14 hands), stocky, thick-coated, hard-hooved, it paws through snow for winter grass, tolerates dehydration, and needs no shoeing. Selection for hardiness, foraging self-sufficiency, and endurance over speed — mediocre sprinter, extraordinary distance animal (60-80 miles/day when remounted). The composite recurve bow is usable from the saddle only because the turghan is trainable to respond to knee pressure. Conversely, the bow made the turghan the state's strategic asset. The Ndowu Buffalo Ndowu [PROP] (Bubalus bubalis, water buffalo — swamp type). Prenasalized nd- onset, round back vowel o, open u final. Tone: low-high (ndo-wu). Plural: bandowu by class-prefix. Co-Evolutionary History The Ndjadi delta alternates deep-flood and cracked-clay drawdown, and the ndowu is the only bovid that thrives across the full cycle. Splayed hooves and flexible pasterns let it plow belly-deep mud where any cow would founder; sparse sweat glands make wallowing obligate. Centuries of selection for draft power over dairy yield produced a stocky swamp-type animal — smaller than upland river-type dairy buffalo, but tractable, surefooted in paddy, and long-lived. The ndowu's true agronomic gift is puddling: repeated passes under yoke churn flooded topsoil into a compacted plow-pan that seals the field against percolation, multiplying the value of every unit of irrigation water. Without the ndowu, the delta's wet-rice economy does not run at scale. A pair is the practical minimum for a tenant household; a team of four marks a landed family. Ngaru-Bon Plateau — Keystone Domesticate The Hlonqa Cattle Hlonqa [PROP] (Bos taurus africanus, Sanga-type cattle of the Nguni lineage). Lateral fricative hl- onset and prenasalized palatal click nq- in second syllable — both diagnostic Ngaru-Bon sounds in one word. Noun-class plural: iziHlonqa (many cattle), uHlonqa (a single named beast). Co-Evolutionary History Descended from ancient Sanga hybridization of taurine and humped stocks. Characteristic cervico-thoracic hump (muscular, set forward), lyre-shaped horns, short glossy coat in hundreds of named patterns, and tolerance for tick-borne disease, heat, and drought no imported breed matches. Selection primarily for hardiness and coat-pattern beauty rather than raw milk yield or carcass weight — a herd is read as a living textile. The mixed woodland-savanna ecology rewards a browsing-tolerant grazer that moves between grass and scrub and survives seasonal drought on body reserves. Hlonqa's central economic role: the interest-bearing capital of the lineage — they reproduce, move, and bind families through transfer. Cultural Role Hlonqa are bride-wealth made animate. The Naluma Tree Naluma [PROP] (Artocarpus altilis, breadfruit). Strict open-syllable CV-CV-CV, low back vowel a with rounded u break, liquid l. No consonant clusters, no closed syllables. A cultivar is a naluma; a grove or lineage-orchard is a nalumarai. Co-Evolutionary History Austronesian colonists carried breadfruit along every leg of the archipelagic expansion because a single adult tree can feed a household for fifty years on almost no labor once established. Clonal propagation from root suckers let founders move selected varieties onto new volcanic islands within a generation of landfall. Centuries of selection produced scores of cultivars distinguished by fruit season, flesh texture, seed-bearing vs. seedless, and trunk straightness and latex yield. The tree solved four problems at once: staple starch, canoe timber, caulking gum, and bast fiber for cordage and tapa-analog cloth. No other Oravan cultivar is simultaneously food, hull, and glue. The volcanic archipelago's thin young soils, rapid leaching, and frequent cyclones favored a deep-rooted, wind-flexible, fast-regenerating tree over cereal agriculture. Design Principles 1. Keystone status chosen for ecological indispensability, not cultural prestige alone. The water buffalo is named for the Ndjadi because puddling wet-rice paddy is non-substitutable work. 2. One civilization gets a tree rather than an animal — Oravan's Austronesian maritime economy pivots on a single multi-use cultivar (breadfruit). 3. Irrah terminology preserved verbatim — rahab, ruhub, arwat, Qeturin. No new name proposed for that slot. 4. All names built from stated phoneme palettes rather than borrowed whole from real analog languages. 5. Tech ceiling 1200-1450 CE — no closed-shed dairy, no herdbooks, no artificial insemination, no shoed horses where analog went unshod. The Q'awa Camelid Q'awa [PROP] (Lama glama, llama). Initial ejective uvular /q'/ — the Qollari signature sound. Back low vowel a, open CV final. Plural by reduplication: q'awaq'awa for a drove, q'awakuna with plural suffix. Co-Evolutionary History The Qollari altiplano is too high for the horse, too cold for the ox, and too steep for the wheeled cart. The q'awa resolves all three problems. Bred from the wild guanaco over four to five millennia, it evolved for cloud-forest and puna pastoralism at 3,500-4,500 m. Its soft two-toed pad puts negligible pressure on fragile ichu-grass soils; high-affinity hemoglobin lets it work above 5,000 m; low water demand matches a glacial-stream landscape. Selection pressure has been for pack endurance over speed: carries 25-30% of body weight 15-20 km/day across passes no mule could cross. Two parallel lineages bred alongside: a finer-boned fiber variant (alpaca analog) and a state-protected wild fiber giver (vicuna analog). Cultural Role The q'awa is the state's logistical spine and religious offering of first choice. Six Nations at One Quay — A Week in the Basin Day One — Dawn at the harbor. You come in on a galley overnight, riding the last of the land-breeze. The harbor takes shape before the sun does. First the bell of the northern merchants' fondaco tolling Prime, then — almost answering from the minaret opposite the Customs Mole — the muezzin-analog's long vowel flattening across the water. Overnight rain has steamed off limestone quays; the smell is tar, wet stone, and the sharper reek of garos — fermented fish sauce the dockside taverns ladle by the thimble. Rigging creaks; a caulker's mallet starts in on a hauled-out galley. Gulls (Larus spp.) quarrel over the night's fish-gutter. The mattanza boats come in heavy with bluefin (Thunnus thynnus) still-bleeding; women sort sardines (Sardina pilchardus), octopus (Octopus vulgaris), flathead mullet (Mugil cephalus). A European shag (Phalacrocorax aristotelis) dries its wings on a bollard. Midday at the Funduq of the Six Nations. The sun has whitened the walls until the eye refuses them. Three Non-Negotiable Rhythms Dawn-Midday-Night Triptych Every biome has a distinct triptych: - First sound (hornbill duet, fish-eagle yelp, muezzin-analog, rooster across a lagoon) - Peak-sun hazard (heat shimmer, reef glare, altitude UV, reg-gravel that eats shoe-leather) - Night-presence (wolves, leopards, karakurt, horned viper, corsair-galleys, malarial quays) Drop one and the biome reads generic. Waystations Are Contracts A waystation is always a three-part protocol (greeting, exchange, reciprocation) and the protocol is never purely symbolic — something tangible moves: - A tambo issues rations by quipu count - A dzimbahwe smith relights his bloomery at dawn; iron hoes are the unit of reciprocity - A rahab-caravan buys water-rights at the foggara outlet in rock-salt and silver - A Kheshkai yam inspects the paiza before rotating horses - A Basin caravanserai shares one courtyard wall between mosque, chapel, and shrine Seasonal Doubling Every region must read as two places. He is reading the grain-drift — the faint striae that every wind-reader knows. He tastes the air for the metallic dryness that foretells qibli, the harmattan-analog dust wind. Today: cold, clean, dry. A winter crossing. Good. In the staging-yard the ruhub groan as the packers heave salt-slabs — each roughly the size of a tombstone, two to a rahab — and lash them with plaited palm-rope. Breath steams. A Seven-Day Crossing of the Kheshkai The first light over the Kheshkai Steppe is not light but cold — a blue, breath-stinging cold that bites even in the Grass Moon of high summer. You wake inside the felt tent to the bitter sweetness of dung smoke — argal, dried sheep and horse pats layered into the central iron stove — and the sour-milk damp of the airag skin swinging from the door-frame, punched by every passer-by to keep it churning. The felt walls, bone-white with chalk on the outside, are warm as a lung within. You step out right-footed — never onto the threshold, which steppe custom calls the neck of the house, and which it is ruinous to tread. Horses are already nosing a seep where dark water wells through Carex sedge and pale rye-grass (Leymus), and the men water them in turns, whistling low; somewhere a Siberian marmot (Marmota sibirica) whistles its own sharp alarm from a burrow-mound crowned in silvery wormwood (Artemisia frigida). Before riding out, the three-bowl protocol: milk-tea, then aaruul (dried curd), then fermented mare's milk. You take it with the right hand, left hand cupping the right elbow. You flick three drops — sky, wind, earth — before you drink.…

Upriver Through the Ndjadi — A Seven-Day Passage Day One — Tidal delta. The dhow leaves saltwater on the ebb, its lateen sail slack in the dead air before dawn. Mist lifts from the brown water in sheets, and the first cry of a fish eagle (Haliaeetus vocifer) — that rising, yelping whistle, thrown back and forth between perches — announces the sun. The smell is wet silt, rotting mangrove, woodsmoke from fishing hamlets where women split catfish (Clarias gariepinus) on split-palm racks. Pied kingfishers hover; a Nile monitor (Varanus niloticus) slides from a mudbank like poured oil. Pirogues arrow out from the reed screens, offering smoked bonga and green oysters knotted on vine. By midday the papyrus (Cyperus papyrus) stands so tall the boat vanishes between green walls. Day Two — First market town. A river port built on a tell of older mud-brick. A caravanserai-on-stilts leans over the landing, its floor three cubits above flood-mark, smelling of sun-cracked palm thatch and drying indigo. The plateau air is cold and mist hangs blue in the shadow-pools beneath the kopjes, those piled granite whalebacks. A pair of southern ground hornbills (Bucorvus leadbeateri) is booming in duet somewhere east, the deep ooomph... ooomph... oo-oo carrying four or five kilometres over the wet grass, answered by a Swainson's francolin (Pternistis swainsonii) going kek-kek-KEK from the kraal thorn. Wood-smoke, cattle-dung smoke, and the rust-blood smell of the smith's lean-to — the waystation's bloomery was relit an hour before sun, and the hammer-ring on anvil is already beating like a slow heart against stone. Iron hoes, axe-heads and spear-blanks lie cooling in sand; they are this waystation's second currency, after cattle-count. The waystation itself is a low dzimbahwe in the southern style: courses of hand-fitted granite laid without mortar. A cattle kraal at the centre; a grain-bin on stilts, mudded against weevils; the chief's hut set behind the inner wall; the smith's forge apart, as the old rite requires — Iron Age…

Passage Through the Archipelago The first watch of a dry-monsoon morning breaks grey over the anchorage. Before the sun lifts above the palms, the lagoon is a sheet of pewter; you hear the village before you see it — the thump-thump-thump of an outrigger paddle on a hollow hull as a fisherman scares baitfish, the wet slap of a net cast, a rooster on the beach answering another across the channel, and from somewhere in the coconut grove (Cocos nucifera), the ratcheting call of hornbills and the argument of lorikeets in a flowering Syzygium. The wind carries damp palm thatch, wood smoke, the green-iron smell of mangrove mud where the aerial roots of Rhizophora apiculata bristle at low tide, and the sweet-resinous breath of Pandanus tectorius drying on a rack. We weigh anchor on the ebb. The air is warm and wet, black with the smell of wet moss. Fog drips from tree-fern fronds; Masdevallia orchids cling to the bark; a sparkling violetear hummingbird (Oreotrochilus estella) hums at a red cinchona (Cinchona pubescens) blossom. The arriero warns you to shake your sandals: in this band alone the pit viper (Bothrops atrox) hunts among the leaf-litter. The Three Master Constraints Three ecological constraints do most of the work in driving continental trade: 1. Irrah's timber absence is the continent's single largest trade driver. No wood means no charcoal means no primary iron, forcing the desert into permanent dependence on Ngaru-Bon bloomeries and making the iron-north/salt-south axis of trans-desert caravan trade structurally inevitable. This is the Saharan reality, not a worldbuilding flourish. 2. The tsetse barrier silently shapes Ngaru-Bon's military and logistical profile. A metallurgical apex with no cavalry and severe pack-transport limits exports gold and iron but cannot project force, pushing its trade outward through the Swahili-coast analog rather than overland. 3. Point-source biota — clove on five islands, nutmeg on one archipelago, vicuna above 3,800 m, frankincense on specific fog-fed escarpments — create monopoly rents that fund entire civilizations. These monopolies are inherently fragile; a single bad volcanic year in Oravan or a failed monsoon on Dhofar would reshape continental politics. Kheshkai — Faction Ecology Institutional Substrate Kheshkai is "Non-institutional" in the typology of magic/06, the only Veydrian civ at this position on the Schism Axis. There are no colleges, no guilds, no lineages in the formal sense; master-shamans take one to three apprentices over a five-to-ten-year horseback apprenticeship; identification is by the hearing-gift, a phonological capacity detectable in childhood. Ngaru-Bon — Faction Ecology Institutional Substrate Ngaru-Bon is "Monolithic" in the typology of magic/06, the only Veydrian civ at this position on the Schism Axis. A single guild — the ancestor-smith federation of click-and-lateral-trained lineages — controls every household that addresses infants in Gyamsgra click-speech, every forge that produces consecrated metal, every shrine that certifies the genealogical binding of consecrated weapons to their lineages. Reform from outside is structurally impossible: the click-and-lateral phonology must be acquired in infancy, the developmental window closes at five to seven years, and no external critic can acquire the register to critique it from inside. The two click types mark different ancestral tiers within guild speech: dental for origin-figures, lateral for maintenance-figures. The Ndjadi ka-tier mortal-ordered entity. Juridical, market-facing, the principle of measurement and exchange. The ka- prefix marks the structured, human-scale cosmological tier. The ka- prefix marks the mortal-ordered tier -- the domain of structured human activity, law, commerce, and correct proportion. Unlike the ra- primordial tier (uncreated, ground-of-being) and the nga- chthonic tier (underground, localized), ka- marks what is built, maintained, and adjudicated by human effort operating within cosmological structure. The labial-velar gb- onset is characteristic of Ndjadi's heavier consonant inventory. In ordinary speech, kagbende names a market-weight standard. Lapam (PROPOSAL) The Ngaru-Bon forge-ancestor. The industrial transition figure -- "works behind the wall the cattle cannot pass." The Ndjadi nga-tier chthonic entity. River-bends, underground waters, the places where flow forgets its direction. The nga- prefix marks the localized, earthbound, subterranean cosmological tier. Name and Etymology Ngandim -- common-use form. Sacred-register form: Nga-Ndímba (prefix nga- + prenasalized root -ndím- "to coil/river-bend" + class marker -ba; breathy medial vowel in liturgical pronunciation). The nga- prefix marks the chthonic tier -- underground, localized, site-specific. Where ra- (Ramwen) names the uncreated source and ka- (Kagbende) names the mortal-ordered structure, nga- names what has sunk below, coiled back, or become bound to a specific place. The prefix is the same one used for localized spirits (nga-beli) in everyday Ndjadi, which creates a deliberate taxonomic ambiguity: is Ngandim a deity or the largest spirit? Scribal colleges disagree. The prenasalized cluster nd- plus the breathy medial in liturgical form make this the most phonologically marked of the three tier-figures in sacred-register speech. Nokul (PROPOSAL) The Ngaru-Bon first-ancestor. Cattle-origin figure -- "struck the first hollow" that cattle answered. The founding act of Ngaru-Bon civilization is an acoustic event: a hollow struck, an animal responding before a person could. Name and Etymology Nokul -- common-use form. Sacred-register form: ǀNoɬa (dental click ǀ- + root -noɬ- "to stretch a skin/to hollow" + class marker -a; the click IS the name in liturgical speech). The radical simplification from ǀNoɬa to Nokul demonstrates the sacred-register concept perfectly: the liturgical form requires a dental click and lateral fricative that non-Ngaru-Bon speakers cannot produce. The common-use form strips these to accessible consonants (n-, -k-, -l), making the name speakable across the continent. Ngaru-Bon practitioners consider the common form a convenience, not the real name -- "you say Nokul; we say what he is." The dental click ǀ- in the liturgical form is the most significant phoneme. Clicks enter Ngaru-Bon infants through parental speech from birth; the acquisition window closes in early childhood. The Oravan Fire-House figure. The fire at the center of the house, the roof-beam junction, the domestic hearth. Not Maawara's hearth-aspect -- a separate, older entity. The Ndjadi ra-tier primordial entity. Not a person in the Oravan sense -- a grammaticalized cosmological position. The ra- prefix IS the theological claim. In ordinary Ndjadi speech, ramwen functions as a proper noun without active prefix analysis. In liturgical speech, the prefix is stressed and separated: Ra-Mwéne, foregrounding the cosmological claim. Scribal-priests who use the wrong tier-prefix for this figure are not making a grammar error -- they are making a theological error with (practitioners say) cosmological consequences. The Basin Composite Reckoning The Aethelian Basin has no calendar. This is not an absence. It is an architecture. Where other civilizations declare time — the Qollari priesthood through khipu intercalation, the Oravan priestess-queen through solstice consecration, the Irrah scholar through isnād-certified star-reading — the Basin receives time. Four ports host six foreign calendars and compose from their overlap a commercial rhythm that no single civilization authored and none can unilaterally amend. The Basin's temporal authority is procedural, not declarative. It does not ask which calendar is correct. It asks which contract was sealed with the seven-stroke Filer's Hand before witnesses who remained for the full cadence. The Composite Year The Basin does not count years. It counts rotations. A Basin "year" is the complete circuit of the Triple-Seal Arbitration Court through four port zones — Tavakh-Qarat, Ki-Mbuhari, Halani-Tamu, Dzong-Tamu — each hosted at the season when that port's ecological and administrative conditions are most stable. This is closer to Xenophanes and Carvaka than to modern atheism. She is not saying "there are no gods." She is saying "what you call gods are natural phenomena that we happen to interact with through trained phonological performance." There is no single calendar. There are many calendars, and their agreement is institutionally normal. This distributed architecture is the deep inversion of Qollari. Where Qollari has one declared system whose schism is catastrophic because everyone is on it, Irrah has many certified systems whose divergence is the default state. A caravan-master who departs on the date certified by one Azmarāʔ scholar and arrives at a Basin port where another scholar's computation prevails does not experience a crisis. He experiences the ordinary texture of Irrah time. The Ndjadi Flood-Pulse Calendar The Ndjadi year is not a circle. It is a pulse — a single annual flood that rises, crests, recedes, and leaves the land either sown or hungry. There is no spring, no summer, no autumn, no winter. There is only the flood, the recession, the growing, and the hungry gap. The calendar is hydrology, not astronomy. The Flood as Year Anchor The year begins when the Floodwatch Augmented Bureaucracy publishes the flood-window prediction. This is not a celebration. It is a ruling. The prediction classifies the coming year as "ordinary," "heavy," or "low" flood, and that classification determines the levy schedule, the harvest-guarantee underwriting terms, and the volume of prefix-notarization the Court of the Three Mouths will process. The prediction is based on gauge-readings from a network of upstream stations whose data is compiled by the Floodwatch and ratified at the River-Lord House Assembly convened the week after publication. The people who certify correct speech. Since correct speech IS prayer, the scribes who control certification hold a functional veto over any public act that requires liturgical authorization. The Grammatical Mechanism Ndjadi sacred grammar maps a three-tier cosmological order onto every noun through prefixes: - ra- -- primordial tier (the oldest, most fundamental things: the delta itself, the original water, the foundational concepts) - ka- -- mortal-ordered tier (human institutions, tools, settlements, everything made by living people) - nga- -- chthonic tier (underground, ancestral, spirit-level entities) A misapplied prefix is not a grammar error. It is a cosmological miscategorization with consequences. The canonical teaching-case parallels the Vedic indrashatru accent disaster: a word intended to mean one thing means its opposite when the accent (or in Ndjadi's case, the prefix) falls wrong. The Ngaru-Bon Smelting-Season Calendar The Ngaru-Bon year has two scales. The long scale — what matters — is counted in ancestor-smith tier promotions: Nokul, Amori, Lapam. A generation is not a span of time. It is a name that may refer to one mortal, a sequence of inheritors, or a fiction the Outside-Forge Network maintains for institutional continuity. Neither the Inner Council nor outsiders can determine which without disrupting the institutional position. The year's most important transition is the opening of the cool-dry-winter smelting season, when the bloomeries relight and iron is made. This is when the continent's steel supply is determined. There are no archivists, no knot-records, no star-tables. The Irrah water-scholar order. A quietist institution whose doctrinal restraint is precisely what makes it the richest and most geographically pervasive religious body on the continent. It is a genealogical record. Dead lineages become fixed points in the sky -- stars, constellations, eclipse-recurrence positions. The calendar's accuracy is simultaneously scientific achievement and ancestor-honoring. Correcting the calendar means revising the genealogical record. When rival calendar-keeper lineages dispute an intercalation (whether to add a corrective day to prevent drift), they are simultaneously disputing whose ancestors occupy which celestial positions. An intercalation error is both an astronomical mistake and an insult to specific dead lineages. Summary Qollari magic is calendrical: ejective consonants bind to specific days in a ritual calendar, uvulars are reserved for solstitial rites. The practitioner produces consonants the general population can also produce -- the real monopoly is over which utterances are licit when, enforced by a khipu-plus-calendar knot-record that only the calendarist hierarchy can read. For phonological detail, see (sacredregisterphonology.Willkaqallu). Political Function Who controls the training pipeline: The calendarist hierarchy. Summary Tavas-Kaj is the Aethelian Basin's trade pidgin -- structurally leveled to remove every marked phonological feature that constitutes a sacred register. No clicks, no pharyngeals, no ejectives, no vowel-harmony constraints, no length-distinctions, no cosmological prefixes. This is exactly why it is trade-useful and magically inert. Loanwords enter Tavas-Kaj stripped of precisely the features that made them sacred. Tavas-Kaj is not a sacred register. It is the anti-register -- the linguistic space where all sacred material becomes costume. Its inclusion in this directory is structural: understanding what Tavas-Kaj strips explains what each register's load-bearing features are. Structure Tavas-Kaj is a contact pidgin (not a creole -- no native speakers, learned as a second-language trade tool). Where the Ndjadi delta's five distributaries braid before the sea. A site of theological contestation without physical confrontation -- the dispute plays out entirely in manuscript-debate. The Two Readings Ndjadi reading: The five distributaries are the cosmological ra-/ka-/nga- triad plus two unnamed waters. The three-tier prefix system maps onto three of the five channels; the remaining two are "unnamed" -- either primordial (pre-prefix, older than the grammar) or fallen (once-named, now forgotten). The site's geography IS the cosmological structure made visible. A partly-submerged stepped platform at the Aethelian Basin's dead center. The most physically contested sacred site on the continent. Currently Oravan-garrisoned with Ndjadi time-sharing access. The Site A monumental stepped structure -- platforms descending into tidal water, the lowest courses permanently submerged, the upper courses exposed at low tide. The construction predates both Oravan and Ndjadi ethnogenesis. Neither civilization built it. Both claim it. The architecture is ambiguous by accident of geology: tidal submersion has eroded lower inscription layers while preserving upper ones, and periodic earthquakes have exposed, re-buried, and re-exposed different courses over centuries. The site is a palimpsest -- every generation's claims are literally carved over the previous generation's, and the tides selectively erase. It is where portable fragments from all six civilizations mix, recombine, and become something that works at the crossroads without belonging to anyone. What It Is The syncretic layer is the religion of people who live between traditions: merchants, sailors, dockworkers, translators, itinerant smiths, caravan guards. The Ancestor-Stone Complex Both Ngaru-Bon and Qollari treat ancestors-in-worked-stone as the civilization's political spine. The material differs -- Ngaru-Bon works metal, Qollari works terrace-stone -- but the principle is the same: ancestors are present in the material they shaped, and the material legitimizes the living through continuity of craft. Ngaru-Bon: Ancestors in Metal For Ngaru-Bon, the forge is where ancestors speak. Lapam -- "the striker" -- is the forge-ancestor who taught the first smith. The named-lineage ancestors (Nokul, Amori) are the cattle-keeper and counter who gave the culture its economic foundation. All three are ancestor-class figures, not deities -- they were people who became politically load-bearing after death. The ancestor-smith guild controls both ritual and military production. A forge-strike -- refusing to produce weapons or reconsecrate tools -- is the institutional lever. This parallels Investiture Controversy mechanics: the smiths don't command armies, but armies can't fight without their products. A local intensification on the Water-Covenant substrate, not a separate tradition family. The Fire-House fuses volcanic fire with the oceanic Water theology to produce something no other descendant of the Water-Covenant has: a dual-aspect divinity whose two media (salt water and volcanic fire) are treated as the same creative-destructive force. Why It's Not a Separate Family The Fire-House does not have its own substrate, its own proto-theology, or its own independent history. It is what happens when the Water-Covenant lands on volcanic islands. The fire was added to the water, not substituted for it. Oravan purification rites, tiered cosmogony, and the Tenth-Water-in-the-body concept are all Water-Covenant features. The fire -- the caldera, the eruption, the hearth -- is the local addition. This distinction matters for cross-civ analysis. When Ndjadi grammarians argue with Oravan priestesses about the Water-Covenant substrate, the fire element is not part of the dispute. The Ndjadi don't contest fire; they contest whether personalizing the Water is a valid development or a corruption. The fire is simply not their problem. Two civilizations -- Kheshkai and Qollari -- share a proto-concept of the Sky as an impersonal mandating order. Each moved in opposite interpretive directions. The shared substrate is NOT a proto-Sky god in the Tengri mold ("Central Asia with serial numbers filed off"). It is a concept: the sky orders, and the ordering can be read. The Substrate The Sky-Mandate substrate holds that the sky imposes order on the world below. This order is readable -- through weather, through star-positions, through seasonal cycles -- and the reading confers legitimacy. Whoever reads the sky correctly has the right to act. Unlike the Water-Covenant, the Sky-Mandate substrate did not leave behind a rich ritual vocabulary or a cosmological taxonomy. What it left is simpler and harder to fake: a shared conviction that the sky's order is impersonal, that reading it is a skill, and that the reading legitimizes action. The disagreement between Kheshkai and Qollari is over what "reading" means. Two Descendants, Opposite Metaphysics Kheshkai: The Sky as WILL Kheshkai reads the sky as a near-person. Site-specific spirits that predate all named traditions. Rivers, passes, specific trees, particular wells, a named wind that blows in a specific wadi in a specific season. Every tradition has variably absorbed or suppressed them. They are the Veydrian equivalent of Shinto kami surviving under Buddhism, or ovoo cairns surviving under Central Asian Islam. What the Sub-Stratum Is These are not gods, not ancestors, not cosmological categories. They are place-entities. A spirit of a specific spring. A presence at a specific mountain pass. The thing that lives in a particular old tree. They have no portfolios, no priesthoods, no doctrines. They have addresses. The sub-stratum provides the ambient numinous texture of the world -- the Skyrim-style enchanted feeling -- without requiring any deity to be real. A traveler crosses a pass and feels watched. A well produces water that tastes different on certain days. A tree that has stood for centuries drops a branch the day a notable person dies nearby. The Water-Covenant Complex The largest and most internally diverse tradition family on the continent. Three civilizations -- Oravan, Ndjadi, and Irrah -- descend from a shared proto-theology that held the cosmos is ordered by the movement and division of waters: surface, underground, sky, dew, and the hidden moisture in living bodies. Ngaru-Bon touches the edge through dew/river rites whose relationship to the main complex is actively debated. The Substrate The Water-Covenant has no founder, no revealed text, no covenant moment. It is recoverable only by inference, like the Vedic substrate or Proto-Indo-European dyeus. In-world scholars disagree about whether it was ever a "religion" or only a shared cosmological grammar. The absence of a founding narrative is deliberate: it prevents any descendant tradition from claiming priority through apostolic succession. What the substrate left behind: - A tiered water cosmology -- the idea that different waters (rain, river, well, dew, bodily moisture) occupy different cosmological registers with different sacred valence - Purification rites tied to water-contact (washing, drinking, immersion, sprinkling) with register-specific protocols…

Veydria Timeline Layer The timeline is a stratigraphic record, not a chronicle. Every epoch is visible through what's left in the ground — re-carved shrines, cognate place-names, disputed inscriptions — rather than through named kings and dates. The continent has no shared calendar. "Years ago" is measured in generations, dynasties, or religious cycles, and these disagree. The model is comparative reconstruction (as in proto-Indo-European studies) plus Braudelian layered time: geography as the slow variable, politics as the fast.
